title: JEZEBEL WAS WICKED—BUT NOT FOR HALF THE REASONS SOCIAL MEDIA CLAIMS
paragraphs:
JEZEBEL WAS WICKED—BUT NOT FOR HALF THE REASONS SOCIAL MEDIA CLAIMS
We turned one of Scripture’s most terrifying women into a stereotype about makeup, confidence, and “difficult women.” The Bible tells a darker story—and if we actually listen to it, we may discover that the spirit we keep accusing others of can hide much closer to home.
Her name has become an insult.
Jezebel.
Say it in certain Christian circles and everybody thinks they know exactly what it means.
A seductive woman.
A woman who wears too much makeup.
A woman who dresses provocatively.
A controlling wife.
A strong woman who intimidates men.
A woman with influence.
A woman who questions leadership.
A woman somebody simply does not like.
Sometimes the accusation becomes even more dramatic: “She has a Jezebel spirit.”

And just like that, a biblical name attached to bloodshed, idolatry, persecution, deception, abuse of royal authority, and unrepentant rebellion against God gets reduced to a convenient religious label we can throw at somebody who makes us uncomfortable.
But there is a problem.
Some of the things Christians routinely say about Jezebel are not what Scripture actually says.
And that matters.
Because when we exaggerate someone’s sins beyond the biblical text, we do not become more biblical.
We become less biblical.
Jezebel was wicked enough without our inventions.
Terrifyingly wicked.
But if we want to understand why, we have to stop listening to social-media mythology long enough to hear the Bible.
The first major introduction to Jezebel comes in 1 Kings 16:31. Ahab, king of Israel, married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and then went and served Baal.
That sentence is not merely telling us about a troubled marriage.
Something catastrophic was entering Israel’s royal house.
Ahab erected an altar for Baal in Samaria. Baal worship was promoted while Israel belonged covenantally to YHWH.
Jezebel was not merely an unpleasant queen.
She became a powerful enemy of the worshipers of the living God.
And Scripture eventually gives us one of the most chilling descriptions of her actions.
When Obadiah secretly protected the prophets of the LORD, 1 Kings 18:4 explains what was happening:
“Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD.”
The Hebrew is brutally direct:
בְּהַכְרִית אִיזֶבֶל אֵת נְבִיאֵי יְהוָה
behaḵrît ʾÎzeḇel ʾet neḇîʾê YHWH
The idea is that Jezebel was cutting off—destroying—the prophets belonging to YHWH.
People were hiding in caves because this woman was persecuting God’s servants.
Let that correct the caricature immediately.
Jezebel's defining evil was not that she knew how to apply eyeliner.
People were hiding from her because prophets were dying.

And somehow we have taken that terrifying biblical reality and turned “Jezebel” into an accusation we sometimes throw at women because of clothing, personality, beauty, influence, confidence, disagreement, or cosmetics.
That should trouble us.
Because there actually is a makeup scene in Jezebel’s story.
It happens shortly before her death.
Second Kings 9:30 says that when Jezebel heard Jehu had arrived, she painted her eyes, arranged her hair, and looked from a window.
And from that one scene, enormous assumptions have sometimes been constructed.
But read carefully.
The text tells you what she did.
It does not say that God condemned her because she painted her eyes.
It does not say cosmetics constituted “the Jezebel spirit.”
It does not say women who wear makeup resemble Jezebel.
It does not establish eyeliner as the theological explanation for her judgment.
Her judgment had already been pronounced before that scene.
Long before she looked out that window, Scripture had documented what she had done.
She promoted idolatry.
She persecuted the prophets of YHWH.
She threatened Elijah.
She participated in a royal system that led Israel deeper into rebellion.
And then came Naboth.
That story should make every person with power uncomfortable.
Naboth owned a vineyard near Ahab’s palace.
Ahab wanted it.
Naboth refused.
Not merely because he was stubborn.
He told the king, “The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.”
So the king went home angry, lay on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat.
Then Jezebel entered.
She discovered why her husband was sulking and essentially told him to get up because she would obtain the vineyard for him.
And this is where the story becomes horrifying.
Jezebel wrote letters using Ahab’s name.
She sealed them with his seal.
She contacted the elders and nobles of Naboth’s city.
She ordered a public fast.
She arranged for Naboth to be placed prominently before the people.
Then she commanded that two worthless men accuse him falsely of blaspheming God and the king.
The accusation worked.
Naboth was taken outside the city.
And stoned.
Dead.
Then a message returned to Jezebel.
Naboth was dead.
Her response was essentially: Go take the vineyard.
Read that slowly.
A man had property the powerful wanted.
He would not surrender it.
So authority was weaponized.
Religion was weaponized.
Witnesses were weaponized.
Public reputation was weaponized.
Legal process was weaponized.
And an innocent man died so powerful people could possess what belonged to him.
That is Jezebel.
Not a woman who simply had a strong personality.
Not a woman who refused to be quiet.
Not a woman wearing lipstick.
This was corruption powerful enough to manufacture guilt and destroy an innocent person.
And here is where this story stops being comfortable.
Because Jezebel becomes very easy to condemn when she remains thousands of years away.
But Scripture was never given merely so that we could stare at someone else’s darkness.
It also shines light into ours.
Maybe you have never murdered anyone.
But have you ever destroyed someone's reputation because you wanted control?
Have you ever repeated something you never verified because believing it benefited you?
Have you ever used spiritual language to punish somebody who would not give you what you wanted?
Have you ever called manipulation “discernment”?
Have you ever called jealousy “concern”?
Have you ever recruited other people into your offense so that somebody else would appear guilty?
Have you ever told only the part of the story that made you look innocent?
Have you ever used the name of God to strengthen an accusation God never told you to make?
Suddenly Naboth's vineyard does not feel so ancient.
Sometimes vineyards look like reputations.
Sometimes they look like ministries.
Sometimes they look like relationships.
Sometimes they look like careers.
Sometimes they look like somebody's dignity.
Sometimes we cannot possess what another person has, so instead of surrendering our envy, we begin building a case against them.
And the frightening thing about Jezebel's scheme was that it looked religious.
She proclaimed a fast.
Think about that.
A fast.
Something associated with humility before God became part of the machinery used to murder an innocent man.
You can use religious language and still be operating in rebellion against God.
You can quote Scripture while destroying someone.
You can say “the Lord showed me” when the Lord said nothing.
You can pray publicly while plotting privately.
You can call something discernment when it is actually suspicion.
You can make another believer the villain of your testimony because acknowledging your own sin would cost too much.
And this is precisely why casually labeling people “Jezebel” can become spiritually dangerous.
The very accusation supposedly meant to expose manipulation can itself become manipulative.
Imagine being a woman in a church who disagrees with somebody in authority and suddenly hearing, “Jezebel.”
Imagine being outspoken.
“Jezebel.”
Beautiful.
“Jezebel.”
Confident.
“Jezebel.”
Wearing makeup.
“Jezebel.”
Setting boundaries.
“Jezebel.”
None of those things, by themselves, establishes the biblical pattern associated with Jezebel.
If we are going to invoke Scripture, Scripture deserves the right to define its own terms.
And yet there is another passage people cannot ignore.
Second Kings 9:22 contains Jehu’s accusation concerning Jezebel. The Hebrew reads:
עַד־זְנוּנֵי אִיזֶבֶל אִמְּךָ וּכְשָׁפֶיהָ הָרַבִּים
ʿad-zenûnê ʾÎzeḇel ʾimməḵā ûḵəšāpehā hārabbîm
It speaks of Jezebel's “whoredoms” and her “many sorceries/witchcrafts.”
That language should not be erased.
But neither should we make it say whatever we want.

In the prophetic world of the Old Testament, sexual-infidelity language can carry both literal and covenantal/idolatrous dimensions depending upon context. Jezebel's story is unquestionably saturated with idolatry and opposition to YHWH. The Hebrew keshaphim language in 2 Kings 9:22 also explicitly associates her with sorceries.
So yes—the Bible gives us very serious categories.
We do not need fabricated ones.
And centuries later, the name appears again.
Jesus addresses the church at Thyatira in Revelation 2.
The Greek text says:
ἀλλὰ ἔχω κατὰ σοῦ ὅτι ἀφεῖς τὴν γυναῖκα Ἰεζάβελ...
alla echō kata sou hoti apheis tēn gynaika Iezabel...
“But I have this against you: you tolerate that woman Jezebel...”
The passage describes her as calling herself a prophetess and teaching and misleading Christ's servants into sexual immorality and eating food sacrificed to idols.
The Greek uses the verbs:
διδάσκει — didaskei — “she teaches”
and
πλανᾷ — plana — “she leads astray,” “deceives,” or “misleads.”
That is crucial.
The New Testament use of the name focuses again on corrupt spiritual influence—teaching that leads Christ's servants away from faithfulness into immorality and idolatrous compromise.
And Revelation says something astonishing immediately afterward.
Christ says He gave her time to repent.
Do not miss that.
Even there.
Even in a passage of terrifying judgment.
Repentance is still mentioned.
That changes the temperature of this entire conversation.
Because Christianity is not ultimately a religion of finding Jezebel in everybody else.
The Gospel asks a far more dangerous question.
What needs to repent in me?
That is where Jesus enters this story.
Because without Jesus, an article about Jezebel becomes another opportunity to feel righteous by studying someone else's depravity.
“She was terrible.”
Yes.
But what are we going to do with ours?
Her idolatry may have been visible in temples dedicated to Baal.
Ours can be hidden behind respectable lives.
Her idol had a name.
Ours might be money.
Approval.
Sex.
Status.
Control.
Influence.
Politics.
A relationship.
A ministry.
Our image.
Our followers.
Even our own theology can become an idol when winning arguments becomes more precious to us than resembling Christ.
Jezebel manipulated a legal process to get Naboth's vineyard.
We manipulate conversations.
She used false witnesses.
We use screenshots without context.
She weaponized accusation.
We weaponize posts.
She wanted control.
So do we.
She could not tolerate the prophetic word opposing her.
Sometimes neither can we.
And suddenly this article is no longer about an evil queen.
It is about the human heart.
Your heart.
Mine.
The heart that knows how to hide rebellion behind explanations.
The heart that knows how to justify bitterness.
The heart that knows how to make its own desires sound holy.
The heart that wants God—provided God does not touch the throne we secretly occupy.
And then comes Jesus Christ.
Not another influencer diagnosing everybody's “spirit.”
Jesus.
The One who knows exactly what is hidden.
The One before whom manipulation cannot hide behind charm.
The One before whom lust cannot hide behind privacy.
The One before whom pride cannot hide behind ministry.
The One before whom greed cannot hide behind ambition.
The One before whom bitterness cannot hide behind “discernment.”
The One who sees every Naboth we have wounded.
Every truth we twisted.
Every person we secretly hated.
Every compromise we protected.
Every idol we fed.
Every room of the heart we hoped He would never enter.
And instead of telling sinners to clean themselves up enough to deserve Him, Christ went to the cross.
This is the scandal.
The Holy One died for the unholy.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The King allowed Himself to be falsely accused.
Think about that after reading Naboth's story.
Naboth was falsely accused and condemned.
Centuries later Jesus Christ would also stand before false testimony.
But Jesus was not merely another innocent victim.
He willingly went toward the cross as the Lamb of God, bearing sin, fulfilling the Father's redemptive purpose.
At Calvary, God did not pretend evil was harmless.
He demonstrated how deadly sin truly is.
And at the same cross, He demonstrated how immeasurable His grace is.
That means the message is not:
“Find the Jezebel.”
The message is:
Repent.
Come home.
Stop hiding.
Bring the idol into the light.
Bring the manipulation into the light.
Bring the sexual sin into the light.
Bring the bitterness into the light.
Bring the false accusation into the light.
Bring the secret addiction into the light.
Bring the religious pride into the light.
Bring the need for control into the light.
And come to Jesus.
Because Christianity does not teach that sinners transform themselves into saints through embarrassment.
We are saved by grace through faith, and the Christ who forgives also transforms.
Grace is not God pretending your sin did not matter.
Grace is God providing in Christ what you could never provide for yourself.
And repentance is not God humiliating you for returning.
It is the sinner finally dropping the weapon, abandoning the idol, and coming home to the Father.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe you expected an article exposing Jezebel.
And somewhere along the way Scripture started exposing you.
It exposed me too.
That is what the Word does.
It refuses to remain a telescope pointed at somebody else's sin.
Eventually it becomes a mirror.
So before you ever call another human being “Jezebel” again, remember what the biblical record actually emphasizes.
Idolatry.
Persecution of God's prophets.
Abuse of power.
False accusation.
Bloodshed.
Manipulation.
Opposition to the word of God.
Sorcery.
And, in Revelation's Jezebel imagery, deceptive teaching associated with sexual immorality and idolatrous compromise.
Those are serious things.
Serious enough that we should never cheapen them into Christian slang.
And there is another truth we need to recover.
Strong women are not automatically Jezebels.
Scripture contains courageous women whom God honored.
Deborah exercised leadership.
Esther risked her life before a king.
Abigail confronted David's destructive anger with extraordinary wisdom.
Priscilla helped instruct Apollos more accurately in the way of God.
Mary Magdalene became a witness to the risen Christ.
Strength is not Jezebel's defining sin.
Female influence is not Jezebel's defining sin.
Beauty is not Jezebel's defining sin.
Makeup is not Jezebel's defining sin.
Her rebellion against God is.
And men should not read this article with smug relief either.
Ahab is standing right there.
Scripture does not permit him to disappear behind his wife's wickedness.
First Kings 21 says Ahab “sold himself to do wickedness” and that Jezebel urged him on.
Ahab wanted the vineyard.
Ahab accepted the fruit of the injustice.
Ahab went down to possess what a murdered man had owned.
God confronted him too.
So the Jezebel story cannot honestly become an excuse for blaming women for male sin.
Ahab answered to God for Ahab.
Jezebel answered to God for Jezebel.
And you will answer to God for you.
I will answer to God for me.
That may be the sentence somebody needed today.
Stop spending your entire spiritual life diagnosing everybody else.
Your husband.
Your wife.
Your pastor.
Your former church.
Your ex.
Your mother.
Your father.
Your political enemy.
The person who hurt you.
The Christian who disagreed with you.
There may indeed be real sin in their lives, and Scripture never requires us to pretend evil is good.
But while examining everyone else, do not neglect the person standing before your mirror.
David prayed:
“Search me, O God.”
Not:
“Search everybody who annoys me.”
Search me.
Know me.
Try me.
See whether there is any grievous way in me.
That is where revival begins.
Not when we discover a new label for somebody else.
When we finally become honest about ourselves before God.
But you also do not have to hide.
Maybe your battle is different.
Maybe you have been falsely labeled, spiritually manipulated, or crushed beneath accusations that Scripture itself never made against you.
Then hear this carefully:
Human labels do not outrank the verdict of Jesus Christ.
Run to Him.
Let Scripture—not somebody's anger—define sin.
Let Scripture—not social-media theology—shape your conscience.
And let Christ—not your accusers—be the center of your identity.
There is no glory in pretending we never needed grace.
The glory is that Jesus saves people who desperately do.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this—not somebody you want to attack, but somebody who has been wounded by careless biblical accusations—send this to them.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
Christ alone saves.
Supporting sound Christian content can help that content reach the exhausted believer scrolling alone at midnight.
The woman who has spent years believing God hates her.
The man hiding an addiction behind Sunday clothes.
The believer who has almost walked away.
The skeptic who still cannot stop thinking about Jesus.
The person who needs someone to open Scripture without turning it into a weapon.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not even believe yet but cannot stop wondering whether Jesus might actually be who Christians say He is.
And please do not leave this merely thinking about Jezebel.
Leave thinking about Jesus.
Jezebel reminds us that evil is real.
Naboth reminds us that innocent people can suffer beneath corrupt power.
Ahab reminds us that allowing and benefiting from evil does not erase personal responsibility.
Revelation reminds us that churches can tolerate destructive teaching.
But Jesus reminds us that judgment is not God's only word to sinners.
“Repent.”
There is still time.
That word is mercy.
The same Christ who exposed sin at Thyatira offered time to repent.
The same Lord who sees through every disguise still calls sinners to Himself.
And the Gospel declares something Jezebel's story could never accomplish by itself:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Not because sin is small.
Because Christ is mighty to save.
Maybe your story has scandal in it.
Real scandal.
Not gossip.
Not rumors.
Your own choices.
Your own rebellion.
Things you would erase if you could.
Things you pray nobody ever discovers.
Things you have never forgiven yourself for.
Listen.
The Gospel was never designed for people with spotless histories.
It is good news for guilty people.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
Jesus Christ calls people to repent and believe.
Jesus Christ forgives.
Jesus Christ restores.
Jesus Christ transforms.
Jesus Christ can take the chapter you thought disqualified you and make it the place where grace becomes undeniable.
So do not spend another night hiding behind somebody else's sin.
Come into the light.
Drop the label.
Drop the mask.
Drop the idol.
Drop the excuse.
Come to Christ.
And remember this when the screen goes dark and you are alone again:
The Gospel is not the story of how well you hid your scandal. It is the story of what Jesus can do when you finally bring it into His light.
